subject: chemistry
title: Catalysts
key_idea: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up. It gives an alternative route with a lower activation energy. More molecules then have enough energy to react, so more collisions are effective.

blocks.text: A catalyst changes the route of a reaction, not its start or end point. This section covers what it does and why the rate rises.

items.meaning: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being changed in chemical composition or amount.
The speeding up of a reaction by a catalyst.

items: The catalyst provides an **alternative reaction route**, with a different mechanism.
The new route has a **lower activation energy**.
More collisions have energy of at least the new, lower Eₐ, so more are effective.
The catalyst is not used up. It is regenerated at the end of the reaction.
It does not change the enthalpy change, or the position of equilibrium.
A catalyst gives an alternative route with a lower Eₐ.
It is not used up overall.
It does not change the reactants, products or enthalpy change.

blocks.text: A reaction profile shows the energy along the reaction pathway. This section covers how to draw it with and without a catalyst.

diagram.alt: Pick the uncatalysed or the catalysed reaction and see its reaction profile, activation energy, enthalpy change and rate.

options.label: Uncatalysed
options.explanation: The reactants must climb the whole energy barrier.

options.label: Catalysed
results: Lower: a lower peak on a new route
options.explanation: The lower route has a smaller barrier. The reactants and products are at the same energy as before.

items: Draw the same reactant and product levels for both reactions.
Draw the uncatalysed route as a higher peak.
Draw the catalysed route as a lower peak, and label both activation energies.
The enthalpy change, ΔH, is the same for both.
Both profiles start and finish at the same levels.
The catalysed peak is lower.
ΔH does not change.

blocks.text: The distribution of energies explains why a lower Eₐ gives a faster rate. This section covers how to show it.

items: Draw one Maxwell–Boltzmann curve at one temperature.
Mark the uncatalysed Eₐ and a second, lower Eₐ for the catalysed route.
The area to the right of the lower Eₐ is bigger.
A greater proportion of molecules has enough energy to react, so the rate increases.
The curve itself does not change, because the temperature is the same.
The curve stays the same. Only Eₐ moves to the left.
A larger area lies beyond the lower Eₐ.

blocks.text: Catalysts are grouped by their phase compared with the reactants. This section covers the two types and why catalysts matter in industry.

items.meaning: A catalyst in the same phase as the reactants.
A catalyst in a different phase from the reactants, usually a solid with gaseous or liquid reactants.

diagram.alt: A sorting activity: decide whether each catalyst is homogeneous or heterogeneous.
diagram.prompt: Sort each catalyst into the correct group.

items.text: Aqueous H⁺ ions catalysing the formation of an ester
Aqueous Fe²⁺ ions in a reaction between aqueous ions
Vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process

items: A **heterogeneous** catalyst gives a surface on which gas-phase reactants adsorb and react. A larger surface area is more effective.
A solid catalyst is easy to separate from the products.
Catalysts allow lower temperatures and pressures, which reduces energy demand.
Less energy from burning fossil fuels means lower CO₂ emissions.
Catalysts often let a reaction use fewer steps or less waste, which makes the process cheaper.
Some catalysts are toxic or hazardous, such as some heavy metal compounds. The benefits to the environment are weighed against this.
Catalysts can be poisoned by impurities, and some are expensive.
Same phase: homogeneous. Different phase: heterogeneous.
Catalysts reduce energy use, costs and CO₂ emissions.
Toxicity of some catalysts must be weighed against these benefits.

checks.q: Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
checks.a: It provides an alternative reaction route with a lower activation energy. A greater proportion of collisions have energy of at least the lower activation energy, so more collisions are effective.

checks.q: State what a catalyst changes and what it does not change in a reaction profile.
checks.a: It lowers the activation energy (the peak). It does not change the energy of the reactants or products, so the enthalpy change is the same.

checks.q: Explain the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous catalyst, with an example of each.
checks.a: A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants, for example aqueous H⁺ ions. A heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, for example solid iron in the Haber process.

blocks.text: Know the sustainability benefits of catalysts and weigh them against toxicity.

items: Lower temperatures mean less energy from fossil fuels and so less CO₂.
Details of the catalysed processes are not required.

blocks.text: Know the use of a solid (heterogeneous) catalyst in gas-phase industrial reactions, and the economic benefits.

items: Gas molecules adsorb onto the surface of the solid, react, then leave the surface.
The surface provides the place for the reaction and a lower Eₐ route.
A lower temperature or pressure cuts fuel and plant costs, and a faster rate raises output.

blocks.text: Be ready to construct and interpret reaction pathway diagrams, and to explain catalysis using the Boltzmann distribution.
